Colonial growth in the Antarctic cheilostome bryozoan Cellarinella watersi proceeds through the iterative budding of feeding autozooids, and the accumulating skeletal mass provides a robust basis for estimating asymptotic body size. Using extrapolation of total dry weight data obtained from field-collected colonies, investigators have estimated that the ultimate dry weight attained by a fully grown colony is approximately 0.8 grams . This value represents the maximum non-reproductive somatic mass a colony can achieve under late-successional conditions, when marginal zooid addition has slowed considerably. The estimate is derived from a series of colonies collected at a single site and should be interpreted with caution, given the pronounced variation in growth form observed across different substrates and current regimes. The extrapolation approach used to derive this value assumes that the relationship between colony surface area and dry weight remains linear beyond the size range of measured specimens, an assumption that warrants further testing with larger colonies. Nevertheless, the 0.8 grams figure provides a useful benchmark for comparing the energetic investment in structural carbonate across species of the family Cellariidae, which exhibit a range of erect, rigid colony architectures. This ultimate dry weight (0.8 grams)  contrasts with values reported for congeneric species from lower latitudes, where warmer, more productive waters may permit faster growth and greater final mass despite comparable colony morphologies. Further work examining colonies from contrasting thermal regimes would help clarify the environmental drivers of size variation in this genus.

Although direct mark-recapture studies are scarce for erect cheilostomes, longevity estimates extrapolated from growth banding in the calcareous skeleton suggest that maximum lifespan can extend to approximately 26 years [am = approximately 26 years] at 0 °C [T = 0 °C]. This value aligns with the extremely slow individual and colonial growth rates observed in Antarctic bryozoans, where a single feeding zooid may live for several years and colony expansion is constrained by brief seasonal pulses of phytoplankton productivity. The 26-year (26 years) [am = 26 years] figure also implies that a single colony may persist across multiple decades, gradually accumulating skeleton and occupying space on hard substrates in a competitive benthic environment at a temperature of 0 °C [T = 0 °C]. Many of the larger colonies observed at study sites likely represent individuals that have survived intermittent ice scour and predation by nudibranchs and sea stars. This extreme longevity stands in contrast to most temperate and tropical bryozoans, which commonly complete their life cycles within a single year.

The attainment of reproductive maturity in Antarctic bryozoans is poorly documented, but for Cellarinella watersi it is tentatively estimated that puberty occurs at around 365 days after birth [tp = around 365 days after birth] of the founding ancestrula, under the same ambient thermal conditions of 0 °C [T = 0 °C]. This rather brief pre-reproductive period, relative to the overall colony lifespan, reflects the early onset of zooidal budding and the modular nature of colonial animals, wherein reproductive zooids (ovicells) can appear soon after the first few autozooids are established. The 365-day interval (365 days after birth) [tp = 365 days after birth] here refers to the time elapsed from the settlement and metamorphosis of the larval stage to the appearance of the first fertile zooid capable of brooding embryos at a temperature of 0 °C [T = 0 °C]. Because this estimate is based on limited laboratory rearing data and indirect field evidence, it remains provisional. Nonetheless, it suggests that C. watersi is capable of initiating reproduction within its first year of life, a strategy that may enhance population persistence in a highly seasonal environment where recruitment events are sporadic.

The ecological implications of the life-history parameters inferred for Cellarinella watersi are substantial when considered within the broader context of polar benthic communities. The combination of an ultimate dry weight of 0.8 grams , a maximum lifespan approaching 26 years [am = 26 years] at 0 °C [T = 0 °C], and the rapid onset of reproduction at around 365 days after birth [tp = around 365 days after birth] portrays a species with a relatively high investment in somatic growth and structural stability, yet capable of early reproductive output. This pattern is consistent with a life-history strategy that balances the need for competitive dominance on hard substrates with the risk of stochastic disturbances such as ice scouring. In contrast to many small-bodied, short-lived Antarctic invertebrates, C. watersi appears to follow a more persistent, stress-tolerant trajectory, albeit one that remains intimately tied to the cold, oligotrophic waters characteristic of the Southern Ocean.

Future investigations into the population dynamics of Cellarinella watersi would benefit from long-term monitoring of tagged colonies, coupled with direct measurements of zooid fecundity and recruitment rates. The provisional parameters of 0.8 grams  for ultimate dry weight, 26 years [am = 26 years] for maximum lifespan at 0 °C [T = 0 °C], and a puberty age of 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth] serve as testable hypotheses that can be refined through experiments in controlled aquaria and field observations. Understanding how these values vary across the species' range will illuminate the effects of local environmental gradients, including food availability and temperature, on life-history evolution in Antarctic bryozoans. Such data are especially relevant in the context of climate change, as even modest warming of the Southern Ocean may accelerate growth and reproduction rates in cold-adapted species like C. watersi, potentially altering competitive interactions within the benthic community.
